usage: Made of 월 (moon) + 요일 (day of the week).
Use the particle 에 for the day something happens.
Put 다음 (next) in front of the day.
examples: I go to school on Monday.
N + 이에요 says what today is.
은 marks Monday as the topic.
nuance: 월요일 is the start of the work and school week in Korea, just like in English. The part 요일 means 'day of the week,' so all seven days end with it. When you say what day something happens, attach 에, as in 월요일에.
mistakes: Saying '월요일 가요' without 에 — for a day, you usually need 월요일에.
Writing it as two words '월 요일'; it is one word, 월요일.

usage: 화 comes from 화(火), and 요일 means day of the week.
까지 marks the ending day or deadline.
examples: I have an appointment on Tuesday.
There is a Korean class on Tuesday.
nuance: 화요일 is the second day of the week, the day after 월요일. The first syllable 화 comes from a Chinese character, but you do not need to know that to use the word. Like the other days, add 에 when you say something happens on Tuesday.
mistakes: Confusing 화요일 (Tuesday) with 수요일 (Wednesday); 화 comes before 수.
Dropping 에: say 화요일에 와요, not 화요일 와요.

usage: 수 + 요일; the middle day of the work week.
에 marks the day of the event.
examples: Do you have time on Wednesday?
nuance: 수요일 sits in the middle of the work week, between 화요일 and 목요일. Many people feel it is the halfway point of a busy week. As with every day of the week, use 에 to mark the time when something happens.
mistakes: Mixing up 수요일 (Wed) and 목요일 (Thu); 수 comes before 목.
Saying '수요일이 있어요' to mean 'on Wednesday'; use 수요일에 있어요.

usage: 목 + 요일; the day before Friday.
examples: I meet a friend on Thursday.
There is a meeting on Thursday.
The day after tomorrow is Thursday.
nuance: 목요일 is the fourth day of the week and the day right before 금요일. People often start looking forward to the weekend on this day. Just like the other days, attach 에 when you say something happens on Thursday.
mistakes: Confusing 목요일 (Thu) with 금요일 (Fri); 목 comes before 금.
Forgetting 에: use 목요일에 만나요, not 목요일 만나요.

usage: 금 + 요일; the last weekday before the weekend.
examples: I watch a movie on Friday.
nuance: 금요일 is the last day of the work week, so many people feel happy and relaxed. The evening, 금요일 밤, is a popular time to go out. As with every day, add 에 when you say something happens on Friday.
mistakes: Confusing 금요일 (Fri) with 토요일 (Sat); 금 comes before 토.
Saying '금요일 봐요' without 에; the natural form is 금요일에 봐요.

usage: 토 + 요일; the first day of the weekend.
examples: I rest at home on Saturday.
On Saturday I usually wake up late.
nuance: 토요일 is the first day of the weekend in Korea, so most people do not work or go to school. It is a common day to rest, meet friends, or travel. Like the other days, attach 에 when you say something happens on Saturday.
mistakes: Mixing up 토요일 (Sat) and 일요일 (Sun); 토 comes before 일.
Dropping 에: say 토요일에 쉬어요, not 토요일 쉬어요.

usage: 일 + 요일; the second weekend day.
examples: I go to church on Sunday.
On Sunday I spend time with my family.
nuance: 일요일 is the last day of the weekend, when many people relax at home or rest before the new week. Calendars in Korea often show 일요일 as the first column in red. As with every day, add 에 to mark when something happens.
mistakes: Confusing 일요일 (Sunday) with 요일 alone, which just means 'day of the week.'
Saying '일요일 가요' without 에; use 일요일에 가요.

usage: An official day off, like New Year or 추석.
examples: Banks are closed on public holidays.
에는 marks the day plus contrast.
Today is a holiday, so I don't go to school.
nuance: 공휴일 is an official national day off when most offices, banks, and schools are closed. It is different from a personal vacation day; everyone gets a 공휴일 at the same time. Big examples are 설날 (Lunar New Year) and 추석 (Chuseok).
mistakes: Confusing 공휴일 (official national holiday) with 휴가 (personal vacation).
Saying '공휴일 닫아요' without 에; use 공휴일에 닫아요.

examples: I have an exam this week.
What are you doing this weekend?
nuance: 이번 주 means the week we are in right now. It pairs with 지난주 (last week) and 다음 주 (next week). Note the spacing: 이번 주 is written as two words, while 지난주 is written as one.
mistakes: Writing 이번주 as one word; the standard spelling is 이번 주 with a space.
Forgetting 에: say 이번 주에 있어요, not 이번 주 있어요.

examples: I'm going on a trip next week.
Next week is a bit free.
nuance: 다음 주 means the week that comes after this one. Use it to talk about plans you have not done yet. Like 이번 주, it is written as two words with a space, and you add 에 to mark the time.
mistakes: Writing 다음주 as one word; the standard spelling is 다음 주 with a space.
Dropping 에: say 다음 주에 가요, not 다음 주 가요.

usage: 지난 (past) + 주 (week), written as one word.
examples: I went to Busan last week.
는 marks the topic, past tense.
I met a friend last Friday.
nuance: 지난주 means the week that just finished, so you usually use it with past tense. It pairs with 이번 주 (this week) and 다음 주 (next week). Watch the spacing: 지난주 is one word, but 이번 주 and 다음 주 take a space.
mistakes: Writing it as two words '지난 주'; the standard spelling is one word, 지난주.
Using present tense; 지난주 usually goes with past, like 지난주에 갔어요.

usage: the morning of the day after tomorrow
Use 가 because 모레 acts as the subject.
examples: I have an exam the day after tomorrow.
The day after tomorrow is Saturday.
I have to turn in the homework by the day after tomorrow.
nuance: 모레 means two days from now, one day past 내일 (tomorrow). Time words like 모레, 내일, and 오늘 usually do not need the 에 particle. It is a handy word for making near-future plans.
mistakes: Adding 에: say 모레 만나요, not 모레에 만나요 — time words like 모레 skip 에.
Confusing 모레 (day after tomorrow) with 내일 (tomorrow).
